Read your repo (pulled it current — it was one commit behind; you're now at b36acd6). Short answer: he measured a line that exists in your repo only as an unverified spec reading, and the number he got is worse than the spec implies.

Where the rule lives in your work

docs/research/counters-and-dram.md:464, in your shire-cache section:

"L3-slave requests take priority over local L2 requests unless l3_yield is set. See Errata 3.2 for sub-bank starvation."

That is a read of the SCspec, not a measurement. It isn't in docs/findings/05-claims.md — your claims ledger has no row for it, no M, no experiment ID. He just supplied one.

His setup is the cleanest possible test of it: one amoaddg counter in shire 0's scratchpad, so the line's home shire is known and that shire is also a competitor. From shire 0 the access is a local L2 request; from the other 31 it arrives as an L3-slave request over the mesh. Exactly the two classes the rule ranks.

What his three numbers actually pin down

1. The priority is total, not weighted. Shire 0 at 6% of fair share means it took 0.19% of all operations, and it "only finished after the other 31 were done." Per-shire that's ~17× worse for the shire that owns the line than for any shire that doesn't. The spec says "takes priority"; the measurement says the local path is effectively starved until the mesh queue drains — despite 43 of the bank's 64 request-queue entries not being reserved for L3 slaves.

2. It's the designed behaviour, not the erratum. Your line points at Errata 3.2 (sub-bank starvation) as the hazard. His per-shire counters show no starvation among the 31 remotes — they split it exactly 1/31. So the asymmetry he found is the arbitration rule working as specified, and the erratum did not fire. That separation matters: it means the fix is the l3_yield config bit (it sits in sc_reqq_ctl next to num_l3_reqq_entries, per your line 268), not a workaround.

3. 60 M atomics/s has to be aggregate, and it prices a global atomic. Per-shire would be 1.86 G/s on a single line; your own note says a sub-bank accepts one request every 2 cycles — 300 M/s at 600 MHz — so per-shire is 6× over a hard ceiling. As an aggregate it's 10 cycles per atomic at 600 MHz (14 if the governor is at 850), i.e. a global atomic occupies the bank for ~5 sub-bank slots, not 1.

What it changes in your existing results

Your docs/et-soc1-notes.md says flag round trips through global atomics cost 355–690 cycles and "depend on where the flag's L3 line lives, not on distance." His result supplies the mechanism and the missing half of the bill: the home shire pays, everyone else free-rides, and the penalty is invisible from the remote side — the 31 remotes see perfect fairness while the owner crawls. Any hot shared line (flag, counter, lock, queue head) placed in a shire that also computes will silently starve that shire's own L2 traffic.

It also puts a crossover on your ~5,000-cycle chip barrier (global atomics + credits, allreduce tree 3.7× faster). At 32 participants the serialization is only 32 × 10 = 320 cycles, ~6% of the barrier — so that barrier is latency-bound, not contention-bound, and the tree's 3.7× win comes from latency. But it flips at ~500 participants. One atomic per minion (1,024) would cost ~10,240 cycles of pure serialization — twice your entire 32-shire barrier. That's a concrete rule his number gives you and yours didn't: one global atomic per shire, never per minion.

Worth noting the convergence: his hackathon win came from replacing the barrier with a dual-hart K-split and a log-depth tree release. Your nocbench says the tree beats the global-atomic barrier by 3.7×. You got there from measurement, he got there from optimization, neither of you knew the other was doing it.

The gap, and the joint experiment

nocbench has pairs, matrix, intra, shift, allreduce, barrier, spin — no many-to-one hot-line test. The barrier --scope chip probe does one atomic per shire, which is 32 operations, not a saturating stream. So this is a hole in your suite, not a duplicate.

And the reverse gap is yours to fill: he has throughput and fairness, no power. A contended hot line concentrates activity in one shire's bank — a spatial term, which is precisely what your per-tile temperature work needs and can't get from a uniform workload. His benchmark plus your rail instrumentation would give the energy cost of a hot line and show where the heat lands. That's a better first exchange than agreeing that the spec was right.

The two questions worth sending back: does flipping l3_yield restore the owner's share, and what does it cost the remotes? — and does the 6% hold when the line is DRAM-backed rather than in scratchpad.

rules.busy: consecutive events < 3 min apart are merged ('active_s'); a longer gap is also merged when the agent is provably blocked: a foreground tool call is in flight ('tool_wait_s', e.g. a blocking until-loop waiting on a card run), the model call is in flight inside an open turn ('model_wait_s'), or the gap ends at a compaction ('compaction_s'); any other gap >= 3 min is idle (e.g. waiting for background agents/workflows or for the human). A gap in which the only calls in flight are loops watching the agent's own workflows or subagents ('watch_waits') is idle too: the subagents' hours count that time. 'tool_wait_lab_s' is the part of tool_wait_s with a card run or lab-machine command in flight. Intervals with no assistant message are dropped. Strict 3-minute-rule busy time = sum of active_s.
rules.strict: events merged into one busy interval when consecutive timestamps are < 3 min apart

rules.dev: Streams the main agent's transcript line by line and keeps each foreground Bash call whose command runs a program on a card, as the first word of one of its commands: a host program (..._host, ..._launcher), the runtime's it_test, the management service's -m/-n/-t queries, ettelem sampling, a run_*.py / run_*.sh measurement script or a make with DEVICE=silicon (a program named through a shell variable set in the same command, D=...; $D, counts as its value). A call's span is its tool_use to its tool_result, so it includes any build or copy in the same command: an upper bound on the time the card was in use. The card is the machine the command ran on: aifoundry2 when local (the session's machine), else the lab machine the command was sent to; on aifoundry1 the card is ET_DEVICES or the claims-v3 scripts' V3_DEVICE (card 0 when neither is set). Excluded: simulator runs, --help, dry runs (V3_DRY=1), the text of heredocs that only write a script, quoted arguments with no space in them (a grep pattern before a script's name), and background calls (their card time is in the data files or queue logs). Subagents are left out: their card work went through the logged claims-v3 queues (agents that only write code may not reach a card), and their commands that match are analysis scripts named run_* re-run from raw data. Writes card_calls.json to $TIMELINE_DIR: The page keeps the parts of these calls that no other interval covers on that card.
rules.note: intervals before the session started (18 September) are left out; one that began before it is cut at its start

highlights.title: The session starts
highlights.caption: Remote control on, the repository cloned, spacesheep set up; at 09:26 the first research request: fine-grained power and latency observability.

highlights.title: The first card use
highlights.caption: At 09:20 a code-loading test and hello world on aifoundry2; the first memory measurements at 09:34; E1 at 09:57, one memory access taken apart by stage and power rail. The first report, Anatomy of a memory access, went out at 10:11.

highlights.title: 179 agents and a usage limit
highlights.caption: The limits-of-observability workflow started 179 agents, 10 to 15 at a time. At 10:33, as the weekly usage limit hit, the count jumped to 52 for one minute: 44 agents started in that minute and 50 of the 52 failed. The run resumed at 11:04, after the reset, and stopped at the session limit at 11:36: 99 of the 179 starts failed. The hub went live at 12:55.
links: Limits of observability · ET-SoC-1 reports hub

highlights.title: The Horace experiment
highlights.caption: A blog post’s random-matrix power experiment reproduced on the chip, rerun at one start temperature and then with strict control; from 08:44 on 21 Sep runs of up to 10 minutes were allowed. 7.7 card-hours.

highlights.title: A second card
highlights.caption: aifoundry3 joins at 12:05 with checks of its clock governor; at 12:12 E20 repeats the strict protocol on it. The DVFS brief went out at 11:51; One hot line stops a shire (13:27) and the on-chip relay page (16:02) followed that afternoon.
links: The DVFS loop and its leakage

Hand it to the next shire: on-chip relay vs DRAM

highlights.title: The energy manual
highlights.caption: A hierarchical catalogue of what each operation costs: first edition 08:17, every instruction on two cards by 11:28, confidence bars from reruns and cards by 13:50. 7.1 card-hours.

highlights.title: Heat per millimetre
highlights.caption: Two workflows research the wire-energy question and try to refute the measurement; the report on the mesh’s energy per bit·mm went live at 16:11.

highlights.title: The report review
highlights.caption: An audit, a fix pass and two more fix rounds, 108 workflow agents in all (up to 20 at once); 18 pages redeployed at 20:41 and again at 20:43.

highlights.title: Validation overnight
highlights.caption: Every analysis re-run from raw data, then PLAN2: a shared chart toolkit, data regenerated and interactive charts, 108 workflow agents through the night; 18 pages redeployed at 07:18.
links: Limits of observability · ET-SoC-1 reports hub

highlights.title: Claims check v3 begins
highlights.caption: Version 3 of the claims check, pre-registered at 09:08; its first passes ran on aifoundry2 and aifoundry3 from 10:01 (11.8 card-hours before the machine fixes, kept as a separate set).

highlights.title: aifoundry1 fixed
highlights.caption: The broken lab machine troubleshot read-only from 12:56, a report at 14:16; fixed and its fix log published at 15:05, made public at 15:12.

highlights.title: The v3 campaign on three cards
highlights.caption: 17:23 on 25 Sep to 06:53 on 26 Sep: aifoundry2, aifoundry3 and aifoundry1 card 1 through the night, 34.2 card-hours of pre-registered passes.

highlights.title: Four cards, then three
highlights.caption: aifoundry1’s two cards join at 17:12 (amendment A2). All four cards were in use at once for 4 minutes in all (17:28, 17:41, 17:45 and 17:56), in smoke tests and a temperature check of card 0; at 17:56 card 0 was excluded because it overheats under load (A4).

highlights.title: The crash root cause
highlights.caption: aifoundry3’s host crashes traced to a log-level race in the runtime, reproduced without a card (E49) and fixed at 23:15. At 06:16 on 26 Sep, 641 host processes of the fixed build ran on the card without a crash.

highlights.title: The visualization pass
highlights.caption: 8 agents and 6 forks survey the pages and add interactive charts (a card selector, calculators, a claim scoreboard); 19 pages redeployed at 00:08.
links: Limits of observability · ET-SoC-1 reports hub

highlights.title: Gathers and scatters (E48)
highlights.caption: Queued behind the campaign on three cards, 03:19 to 09:22 on 26 Sep: 3.6 card-hours.

highlights.title: The three-card page updates
highlights.caption: 15 agents and 12 forks fold the campaign’s results into every page; ten commits at 08:37 on the pages branch.
links: Limits of observability · ET-SoC-1 reports hub

highlights.title: The weekly limit
highlights.caption: At 08:41 on 26 Sep the account reached its weekly usage limit, and this session’s agents paused until it reset at 11:00 on 27 Sep. The cards finished their queues by 09:22, and another Claude session made 21 commits that evening, 16:00 to 23:26.

highlights.title: Chip diagram and this timeline
highlights.caption: The owner asks for an interactive chip diagram for a talk, this timeline and experiments on heat placement; 4 workflows start by 11:17.

highlights.title: The chip diagram and the PCIe link
highlights.caption: An animated chip schematic for the talk went out at 13:39. The owner’s feedback at 14:08 asked, among other things, to measure the PCIe link it called “not measured”: E50 measured it on three cards, 14:24 to 15:13 (15 runs of about 14 s), and its page went out at 18:09 with the diagram’s second version (commit 18:10).
links: The PCIe link and the launch path

highlights.title: Heat placement
highlights.caption: Does the thermal throttle follow the mean of the die’s sensors or one hot shire, and does the same work placed at the die’s edges run longer before it? Designed, critiqued and pre-registered by 3 workflows; the owner’s decisions at 12:49. Development on aifoundry3 from 16:52 to 22:10, then aifoundry1 card 1 from 20:24, its validation passes from 23:45 to 07:49; aifoundry2 ran 2 short sessions, the first at 16:50. 4.5 card-hours in all.
links: Where the work sits: placement and the thermal trip

highlights.title: The chip diagram polished
highlights.caption: At 20:15 the owner asks for a more professional walkthrough and zoom, then another pass over the pages: 8 agents polish the diagram (motion, a visual system, the tour; commit 23:52) while 9 agents add charts and fix correctness across the observability pages (commit 21:51). At 22:24 the zoom still jumps; 3 agents trace it to the page’s own drawing, and the smooth zoom goes out at 00:20.

highlights.title: DV2: the governor and heat
highlights.caption: At 21:47 the owner asks for another set of DVFS and heat experiments. Theories, a design and its critique came before any card work; the development night on aifoundry2 ran 00:39 to 02:54: 21 read-only watch cycles, 3 sessions and 1 smoke launch, 1.0 card-hours. Development only: the validation plan was frozen afterwards; its queue started at 20:45 on Mon 28 Sep (the last highlight).
links: The DVFS loop and its leakage

highlights.title: aifoundry2 hangs
highlights.caption: In the DV2 session that began at 02:50, aifoundry2’s Master Minion stopped taking work: the second launch never started its kernel, and the next could not reach the command queue. The queue stopped at 02:54. No reset was attempted then, by the lab’s rules; the card came back at 08:32, after the owner approved a reset (below).
links: The DVFS loop and its leakage

highlights.title: Memory levels, interactively
highlights.caption: At 20:37 the owner asks for an interactive diagram of each memory level, down to the transistors, with what nobody knows added to the asks for the team. 16 agents in two workflows built them; the page went out at 05:07, with the hub and the chip diagram updated a minute later.
links: Anatomy of a memory access, interactively

highlights.title: The status, and every task at once
highlights.caption: At 06:14 the owner asks for the status and for parallel agents to finish every open task: a workflow of 22 agents runs from 06:16 to 08:37 (the heat report and its verdicts, a sweep of the review’s open items, an earlier refresh of this timeline, and a rebuild on aifoundry1).
links: Where the work sits: placement and the thermal trip

highlights.title: Machine fixes, and aifoundry2 back
highlights.caption: At 06:33 the owner lets the machine-level fixes that were waiting go ahead: 10 agents export aifoundry3’s system log and raise its size cap, install the new card-holder and health-check tools on the three machines, free 2.4 GB on aifoundry1 and stop orphaned browsers. The owner approves resetting the hung card at 06:35: the per-card sysfs reset re-attaches it but the Master Minion stays hung; after a second approval at 08:32 the management reset brings it back at 08:32, and a test kernel runs cleanly. At 06:39 the owner asks that the requests for the lab lead keep only what needs the team (5 agents).

highlights.title: Heat placement: the verdicts
highlights.caption: The validation on aifoundry1 card 1 ends at 07:49: 10 blocks, all valid. Short bursts pass (the same work on the perimeter took 2.04 times as long to heat the die as in the interior, 5 of 5 blocks); the primary sustained test is inconclusive (7 of its 10 runs met the 150 s cap), so under the frozen rules no theory survived and none was refuted. The report goes out at 09:07.
links: Where the work sits: placement and the thermal trip

highlights.title: The effect of overheating
highlights.caption: At 08:41 the owner asks what temperatures processors are built for, whether a limit should watch the average or the hottest spot, what heat does to switching speed, and why a hot chip stops and then recovers. 11 agents research it (69 sources, 60 of them outside), test it and write it up; E53 ran on aifoundry3 and aifoundry1 card 1 from 10:11 to 12:04 (3.2 card-hours): the hottest sensor ran 1–3 °C above the mean, and 663 checked launches up to an 81 °C mean computed nothing wrong. The page goes out at 13:41.

highlights.title: The walkthrough on phones
highlights.caption: At 09:07 the owner reports the chip diagram cut off on a phone. 4 agents find the cause in the page itself (a minimum width, and a scroll to the middle of the canvas), not in the host; the phone layout, the whole die in the width, goes out at 12:04, and the host’s comment tab over the page’s left edge is reported to its team.
links: Anatomy of a memory access, interactively

highlights.title: The timeline refreshed
highlights.caption: At 13:55 the owner asks to bring this timeline up to date with the latest experiments; the refresh goes out at 14:08, and again at 14:29 and 14:38 after the owner’s two notes on it (14:23: lead each message with what it asked, the timing in small print; 14:35: link the pages each highlight produced).

highlights.title: Requests from the pages themselves
highlights.caption: At 14:10 the owner has the session listen for messages written on the published pages, in their Talk tab: 7 arrive by the snapshot. The memory levels get light tints instead of dotted and striped backgrounds (commit 14:22); the chip diagram gets an eleventh data flow, B, Broadcast (Q62, asked at 14:51, live at 15:59); one message is feedback meant for the spacesheep team.
links: Anatomy of a memory access, interactively

highlights.title: The superseded energies folded in
highlights.caption: At 16:00 the owner points out the sections still marked “energies superseded”. 3 agents fold the newer energies into the memory anatomy, memory hierarchy, on-chip communication and matmul pages (commit 16:45), then sparse compute’s power from three cards and the first pass’s leftovers (commit 17:33); 11 pages go out at 17:36.

highlights.title: Heat per mm: the 2× gap (Q63)
highlights.caption: At 16:09 the owner asks, from the heat-per-mm page, which process node the cited wire-energy figure is for and whether a 2× gap between it and the measurement is expected. 12 agents and forks read the figure’s papers, talks and interviews and the NoC energies measured on other chips; the answer is committed at 17:29 and live at 17:32. At 18:38 the owner asks for a light cyan background: live at 18:39.

highlights.title: A major pass, and this timeline in the repository
highlights.caption: At 20:41 the owner asks for a major pass now that the lab works again: every remaining lab fix and check, the NoC validation, the to-do list, and this timeline committed to the repository. At 20:51 four of the lab report’s host fixes go in on aifoundry1, owner-approved (among them a headless default and unused desktop services turned off); the rest, on all three machines, wait for the owner, since the session’s permission check refused them. A workflow of 8 agents studies the NoC’s voltage control, a wire benchmark, a lab-wide audit and the lab tools, then designs the NoC-voltage experiment and its runner; another of 4 moves this page and its tools into the repository, with a privacy scan of its data (commit 21:52, live at 21:52).

highlights.title: DV2 validation: sessions and verdicts
highlights.caption: The DV2 validation on aifoundry2 ran under its frozen plan from 20:45 on 28 Sep: a read-only temperature reading every 3 minutes, and a heating session only when the card was cool enough. 3 replication sessions ran, 22:13–22:30, 22:42–23:06 and 23:19–23:56 on 28 Sep, each starting at 59–60 °C, with 1, 2 and 4 complete test blocks; the Master Minion, which hung on the development night, kept taking work. No session started after that; the readings (403) went on until the plan’s 20-hour window closed at 16:56 on Tue 29 Sep. Reduced at 16:58: TH3, TH4 and TH8 survived and TH7 fell (1 of 52); TH1, TH2 and Q2 stayed untested, with no run that fits the hottest shire.
links: The DVFS loop and its leakage

highlights.title: NV: the NoC validation, frozen and waiting
highlights.caption: The NoC validation the owner asked for (E54): does the mesh’s energy per bit·mm follow its 0.485 V supply, as heat per mm’s answer to Q63 assumed? A read-only probe of aifoundry3 at 22:54 finds the NoC rail at 485 mV and 400 MHz; at 23:06 the predictions are frozen and the experiment registered, before any card write. The first voltage write, 540 then 600 mV and back, did not start: the session’s permission check refused a command that changes a shared card’s state, so it waits for the owner. The validation is planned on aifoundry2 after DV2.

highlights.title: Four experiments, developed and validated
highlights.caption: 12 agents build and pre-register four experiments on the hub’s open questions (commit 23:47). Each is developed on aifoundry1 card 1 (23:47–00:53), frozen, then validated on aifoundry3 (00:04–01:06), 1.2 card-hours in all. E55: two host-to-card copies in flight in one stream move 0.49 of what one moves at 64 MB, while one in each of two streams loses nothing, and a host write lands in the L3. E56: read replies go y first and write requests x first on both cards, where the chip diagram assumed x first for every route; a link saturates near 92 GB/s. E57: the DRAM bank and row map and per-controller refresh hold on aifoundry3, the L2 keeps TensorLoad lines, and stride-256 runs at 0.665 of the bandwidth; no theory of the 128 B per cycle cap survives. E58: the rails’ meters filter with a time constant of 1.01–1.06 s on every rail of aifoundry3 (0.54 s on card 1’s SRAM rail). The PCIe runner’s first card run since its lock fix, at 23:56, exits cleanly.
links: Limits of observability · ET-SoC-1 reports hub
The PCIe link and the launch path

highlights.title: Sparse parity: from research to the card
highlights.caption: At 21:14 on 28 Sep the owner queues the next task: a sparse-parity solver that uses the chip’s thousand cores, prototyped at toy sizes first and then scaled to the whole chip. A workflow of 5 agents (21:21–22:53, no card) surveys the literature, maps the problem onto the chip and designs it: a noisy sparse parity found by exhaustive correlation, computed as int8 tensor products. 4 more workflows (17 agents) build and tune it. On the card, M1 at 04:21 on 29 Sep solves L1 and L2 with exact checksums, about 5× one CPU core; M4 at 08:42 runs 8–9× one core and 1.0–1.6× six tuned AVX-512 threads; M5 at 11:41, a two-stage screen, solves L2 in 0.323 s and (256,5) in 1.52 s (1.6× and 1.2× six tuned threads at equal loss), at 5.0, 16.6 and 89 J a solve, 2.5–7.7× below the CPU package’s assumed energy. The page went out at 12:41 and was made public at 13:27 (Q67).

highlights.title: A third card for E55–E57
highlights.caption: With the DV2 validation over, aifoundry2 ran three of the major pass’s experiments as a third card, 16:59–17:38 on 29 Sep (15 passes, smoke tests first): E55 pcie2, E57 memp2 and E56 nocr, under the frozen plans. The two-copy results held (T35-S, T34-A), read replies go y first there too, the tensor reload and per-controller refresh hold, and the DRAM map misses one condition on this card (commit 17:38). E58 tau was not repeated on it.
links: The PCIe link and the launch path
Anatomy of a memory access, interactively

highlights.title: The weekly limit, again
highlights.caption: At 18:10 on 29 Sep the account reached its weekly usage limit again, which would reset on 4 October: the agents stopped mid-task. The session stood still until 12:41 on 30 Sep, when the owner continued it on a new account and asked for the unfinished work to go on with agents in parallel.

highlights.title: New user? Start now
highlights.caption: At 13:22 the owner asks for a “New user? Start now” page: self-contained instructions a newcomer hands to their coding agent, from the week’s lessons. 6 agents write it; it goes out public at 14:02. At 14:08 the owner asks for it much shorter: only what the person must do, and a diagram of the three machines and four cards; at 14:24, for one prompt with only a name to fill in. The fourth edition, with an onboarding script a new user runs as themselves, is committed at 16:10.
links: New user? Start here: the AI Foundry ET-SoC-1 lab

highlights.title: The lab dashboard
highlights.caption: At 12:51 the owner asks for a live view of the lab: the three machines, the four cards and the people using them. 8 agents build a collector (the lab tools, who is logged in, their Claude and spacesheep sessions, and a card sample that is off by default) and an updater that republishes the page on every change and every 10 minutes (commit 14:20). The page was published private, and made public that afternoon (below). At 14:29 the owner asks for a view for everyone, with each card’s use over 24 hours, and at 14:58 for each machine’s own state, since aifoundry1 was down and the page did not show it.

highlights.title: Logging who uses the cards
highlights.caption: At 14:29 the owner asks to log who uses each card, for every user old and new, so that the dashboard can show the last 24 hours: an agent builds a card-usage logger (14:37–15:31), and a workflow of 5 agents reviews it and its installation on the machines (15:31–17:21).

highlights.title: Running without the heatsink (Q70)
highlights.caption: At 17:30 on 29 Sep the owner asks whether a card can run without its heatsink, with a sensor or a thermal camera pointed at the chip. Two research agents start at once and stop at the weekly limit; on 30 Sep 2 workflows (8 agents) build, review and finish the report: a model on the record (leakage, the fitted heatsink, a Monte Carlo of the bare package, card 0’s guard samples) and 43 outside sources. A bare card at 600 MHz almost never settles (1 of 3,600 draws), a sensor would see a plated lid at nearly one temperature, and a thermocouple taped to the heatsink’s base is the safe way to read the package. The page goes out at 14:41, cross-linked from four others.
links: Feasibility of running the ET-SoC-1 without its heatsink

highlights.title: The link retrain hang and the power cycle
highlights.caption: At 14:41 on 30 Sep the owner’s session (the neighbor session, in a lane of its own) ran the link test from the lab report on aifoundry1 card 0: a retrain of its PCIe link at 8 GT/s. The whole host hung, both cards with it, until the lab lead power-cycled all three machines at about 15:07. The reboot of aifoundry2 stopped this session and the neighbor and cleared /tmp there: about 19 GB of working files, this timeline’s working folder among them, so working files now stay out of /tmp. Back at 15:18, the neighbor read the boot records and the link’s counters (a hard hang, not a panic), published the incident page at 15:21 and committed the lesson at 15:24: never retrain or re-speed a card’s link on a running host.
links: A PCIe link retrain hung aifoundry1

highlights.title: The driver race reported (Q86)
highlights.caption: At 17:45 on 30 Sep the account reached its session limit, and the agents stopped mid-task. At 20:49, after the reset, the owner continues the session with many agents in parallel, and asks for the driver race that the logger’s review had found to be reported upstream and in the report for the lab lead: the card’s queue counters, which any user can read, are walked without a lock, so a read during a card reset can return garbage. An agent (20:53–21:12) adds it to that report’s requests (republished at 21:14) and drafts the upstream issue for the owner to file: a public version, and the full analysis with a patch to send to the driver’s maintainers privately.

highlights.title: The logger installed, the dashboard public
highlights.caption: At 20:54 on 30 Sep the card-usage logger goes onto all three machines, after 5 agents reviewed it for security, card safety and correctness (15:31–17:21): a small service that records which user’s program holds each card, so that the dashboard can draw each card’s use over 24 hours. The dashboard’s rewrite, reviewed by 6 agents for privacy, the machines’ liveness, the card-use data and the reader, is committed at 21:11: the same view for everyone, who is logged in and doing what, each card’s use and each machine’s own state. It is public, as the owner told the neighbor session at 15:55; at 15:57 the neighbor had stopped its updater from making the page private again.

highlights.title: A departed user’s checkpoints deleted (Q87)
highlights.caption: At 22:23 on 30 Sep the owner asks to free aifoundry1’s disk, which was nearly full, by deleting a departed user’s large public model checkpoints, which can be downloaded again. After a dry run, at 22:25 the 27 checkpoints of 1 GB or more are deleted (118 GB of public models): /home goes from 99% to 72% full, and the pool from 95% to 71%. An agent updates the texts that still called the disk nearly full (22:26–22:37), the New user page is republished at 22:37, and the record is committed at 22:38.
links: New user? Start here: the AI Foundry ET-SoC-1 lab

highlights.title: How low can the clock go? (Q81)
highlights.caption: At 15:34 on 30 Sep the owner asks how far down the clock can go, 100 MHz or even 10 MHz, to run a card without its heatsink under the thermal camera: the envelope of what is possible. A workflow of 16 agents studies it (15:36–23:15): notes on the firmware’s clocks, outside sources, a power and imaging model, reviewed for physics, sources and the reader. The answer is in the heatsink page at 23:17: 100 MHz is the lowest clock the firmware can set (10 MHz cannot be set), and at 100 MHz a card still idles at 19–24 W, so a bare card settles only with a fan or a blower, and only from some cold starts. A camera through a taped lid would see a coarse pattern with lock-in; the recommended route keeps the heatsink and reads the chip’s own sensor with lock-in. The measurement plan is pre-registered, not run.
links: Feasibility of running the ET-SoC-1 without its heatsink

highlights.title: Memory levels: the level tabs zoom (Q82)
highlights.caption: At 15:44 on 30 Sep the owner asks the memory-levels page to zoom smoothly, out and back in, when a level tab or a part is tapped, on phones too, as the arrow keys do on a desktop. A first build (15:45–17:45) is redone on the smoother camera that had just replaced the page’s own: from 20:52 a workflow of 6 agents ports it (commit 22:18), reviews it on a phone, on a desktop for the keyboard and screen readers, and in code, and fixes what the reviews found (00:16 on 1 Oct). Live at 00:36: a level tab or a tap glides out to the common scale and back in to the chosen level.
links: Anatomy of a memory access, interactively

highlights.title: The chip diagram’s powers of ten (Q85)
highlights.caption: At 16:25 on 30 Sep, with a photo of the lab’s rack, the owner asks the chip diagram to zoom like the powers of ten: double-click any part to zoom in, a wide button to go up, out past the card to the rack, the city, the Earth and the galaxies, and in to the circuits. A workflow of 18 agents (16:28–02:22) builds it in phases (a path camera at 21:08, the Up bar and glides between shires at 21:29, the outer and inner scales at 00:14 on 1 Oct), then reviews it for facts, interaction, visuals and code and fixes what the reviews found. Merged and live at 02:23: a ladder of 33 scales, from beyond the observable universe through the Local Group, the Earth, San Francisco, the lab, the rack and the card to the die, and inside it to the 6T cell, the latch, the full adder, the FinFET and the silicon crystal; 131 of 131 tours pass on a desktop and a phone.

highlights.title: aifoundry2’s card falls off the bus
highlights.caption: At 09:42 on 1 Oct aifoundry2’s card stops answering on PCIe while idle: its cooling follows the host’s fans, which slow down when the host is idle. A full-reset reboot at 06:45 on 2 Oct brings it back, but idle it runs away again (126 °C at 07:42); a plain reboot at 10:47 leaves it off, a full reset at 10:53 brings it back, and at 12:02 it falls off for good after heating from 45 °C to a 138 °C mean and 134 W. Out of service since: the air that reaches it is too warm, a fix of the fan settings on site.

highlights.title: Antigravity on the lab machines
highlights.caption: At 16:02 on 4 Oct the owner asks for Google’s Antigravity CLI on the lab machines, reachable from its web dashboard. highlights.title: The lab lead’s report checked; the driver race filed upstream
highlights.caption: On 4 Oct a session on the owner’s second Claude account goes through the report for the lab lead item by item: what a 2 Oct rebuild had dropped comes back at 12:33, the live monitor reads the cards more gently, a card-open logger goes onto aifoundry1, and card 0 is counted again once fixed. highlights.caption: At 21:02 on 4 Oct the owner asks for the machine’s whole agent setup, two Claude accounts with remote control and the Antigravity daemon, with its lessons, to be kept in GitHub, so that the machine can be rebuilt if it is wiped: a private repository with a rebuild guide, committed at 21:17.
